open_alex.title: Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?
open_alex.abstract: SWE-Bench-Verified, a dataset comprising 500 issues, serves as a de facto benchmark for evaluating various large language models (LLMs) on their ability to resolve GitHub issues. But this benchmark may overlap with model training data. If that is true, scores may reflect training recall, not issue-solving skill. To study this, we test two Claude models that frequently appear in top-performing agents submitted to the benchmark. We ask them to find relevant files using only issue text, and then issue text plus file paths. We then run the same setup on BeetleBox and SWE-rebench. Despite both benchmarks involving popular open-source Python projects, models performed 3 times better on SWE-Bench-Verified. They were also 6 times better at finding edited files, without any additional context about the projects themselves. This gap suggests the models may have seen many SWE-Bench-Verified tasks during training. As a result, scores on this benchmark may not reflect an agent's ability to handle real software issues, yet it continues to be used in ways that can misrepresent progress and lead to choices that favour agents that use certain models over strong agent design. Our setup tests the localization step with minimal context to the extent that the task should be logically impossible to solve. Our results show the risk of relying on older popular benchmarks and support the shift toward newer datasets built with contamination in mind.

Resolves 426 of 500 instances under the official swebench.harness.run_evaluation grader. open_alex.title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced LLM Coding Benchmark
open_alex.abstract: SWE-Bench is widely used to evaluate whether large language models can resolve real-world GitHub issues, yet the quality of its benchmark instances remains underexplored. We present SWE-Bench+, an enhanced benchmark framework that improves evaluation reliability by addressing two risks: solution leakage in issue descriptions and weak tests that allow plausible but incorrect patches to pass. We analyze 217 commonly resolved issues from SWE-Bench Lite and SWE-Bench Verified across three top-performing agents, yielding 651 model-generated patches. Our analysis identifies five recurring quality-problem patterns under solution leakage and weak tests. We further develop SoluLeakDetector, which detects solution-leaking content, and TestEnhancer, which strengthens validation tests. We find that 60.83% of commonly resolved issues contain solution leakage and 77.88% are problematic overall. SoluLeakDetector achieves 80.45% accuracy, while TestEnhancer identifies plausible patches for 97.11% of weak-test issues and reduces average resolution rates by 27.00 percentage points on Lite and 36.27 percentage points on Verified.

open_alex.title: Incorporating Data Dependencies and Properties in Difference Verification with Conditions (Technical Report)
open_alex.abstract: Software changes frequently. To efficiently deal with such frequent changes, software verification tools must be incremental. Most of today's approaches for incremental verification consider one specific verification approach. One exception is difference verification with conditions recently proposed by Beyer et al. Its underlying idea is to determine an overapproximation of those modified execution paths that may cause a new property violation, which does not exist in the unchanged program, encode the determined paths into a condition, and use the condition to restrict the verification to the analysis of those determined paths. To determine the overapproximation, Beyer et al. propose a syntax-based difference detector that adds any syntactical path of the modified program that does not exist in the original program into the overapproximation. This paper provides a second difference detector diffDP, which computes a more precise overapproximation by taking data dependencies and program properties into account when determining the overapproximation of those modified execution paths that may cause a new property violation. Our evaluation indeed shows that our more precise difference detector improves the effectiveness and efficiency of difference verification with condition on several tasks.

open_alex.title: Metamorphic Coverage and Reward Sensitivity in Agent Programs
open_alex.abstract: We test whether a repaired verifier accepts archived agent programs that fail fresh, reference-qualified input probes. The study covers 100 programs for one session-window component. Before execution, we freeze 120 traces combining six source-name bijections, five positive event-time scales and four offsets. A shipped reference and two planted controls qualify the harness. Each case runs in a fresh isolated process. All 12,000 program–case executions complete. Ninety-eight programs match every declared contract vector; two differ at identity and every transformed case. All 100 satisfy own-anchor equivariance. Source inspection explains the two differing vectors through alternative event-count idleness policies, which the short task design does not fully resolve. The 119 nonidentity cases add no departures among identity-conforming programs. Replication of baseline-to-repaired scoring changes two labels and ten standardized reward coefficients on fixed evaluation cohorts; probe augmentation changes none. A census of 794 public records supplies archival context. The measurements concern saved programs and include no policy update. We propose an unrun matched private-task experiment to test whether verifier repair improves training outcomes at a defensible cost. Materials. The PDF, editable source, vector figures and sanitized observations accompany the reproduction code. Public benchmark material remains evaluation-only. This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Computational assistance. OpenAI Codex, including GPT-6.1-Sol, assisted study design, literature review, implementation, analysis, figure generation and manuscript preparation. Reported measurements come from logged code executions; the record includes the code and observations needed to reproduce the analysis.

open_alex.title: What Does a Repair Statistic Measure? A Claim-Indexed Audit of Repository-Level LLM Repair
open_alex.abstract: Repository-level repair systems emit many logged events before a verifier pass. A rate over one event is easy to misread when the report omits the event's operational meaning, opportunity budget, support unit, or verifier boundary. We introduce a claim-indexed measurement model that binds each repair statistic to five coordinates: construct, opportunity design, unit of support, endpoint interpretation, and instrumentation provenance. We instantiate the model in a retrospective audit of 2,400 executions: two 30-task DeepSeek strata with disjoint task IDs and a 30-task GLM boundary stratum that reuses the clean task surface. A field-integrity audit identifies 12 raw GLM action positives that conflict with the patch-application evidence required by the governed-action construct. The harmonized table contains no verifier pass outside the governed-action state, while conditional endpoint yield is 14/199 (7.04%) and 14/204 (6.86%) in the two DeepSeek strata. Under eight retained opportunities per fixed cell, governed-action discovery reaches 40.83% and 46.67%; verifier-pass discovery reaches 4.17% and 1.67%. The 28 passing rows reduce to seven positive cells, three tasks, and two task families. Endpoint controls produce the expected result for all six gold runs, six no-op runs, and nine reference-derived mutants. These findings show that repair evidence cannot be reduced to one success scalar. Field semantics, opportunity, support, verifier scope, and instrumentation determine what a reported number measures and which comparisons it can sustain.

open_alex.title: ProofDebt: When Does Memory Improve Continual Software Repair?
open_alex.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly expected to work on the same repository over time, yet most evaluations treat every issue as a fresh start. This makes a basic question hard to answer: when should memory help? We introduce PROOFDEBT, a continual-repair protocol whose memory is built from native-test outcomes, changed files, dependency links, and patch status rather than self-written summaries. A primary campaign contains 891 repair attempts across 11 three-step ChainSWE chains and three model families. Across 1,188 token-matched later-step attempts, PROOFDEBT improves success over reset by 6.6 percentage points, but the average hides an important difference between tasks. Two coders independently audit all 22 later-step tasks and agree on 19 of 22 information-need labels before adjudication (86.4%; unweighted Cohen’s κ = 0.77). Their consensus audit identifies seven tasks where the correct repair genuinely needs information from an earlier repair. On these tasks, reset succeeds on 14.3% of attempts, PROOFDEBT on 60.3%, and an oracle memory condition on 82.5%. On the other 15 tasks, the three conditions remain within 4.5 points. A trace audit shows that practical ledgers usually contain the right obligation but often fail to present it as something the model must preserve. These results suggest that continual-agent evaluations should measure whether a task offers a real opportunity for memory before averaging memory effects.

open_alex.title: Verification and Self-Improvement in Agentic AI: Foundations and Limits
open_alex.abstract: A self-improving agent can find accepted solutions more often without expanding the tasks its verification interface can accept. We extend task-relative verification with explicit support and transcript interfaces to distinguish search gains from changes in accepted-task coverage. A stage's native reach contains tasks accepted with default support; its closure frontier contains tasks accepted with any support the declared interface permits. A semantic containment criterion identifies the authority or exposure condition that every verified escape must violate, while guard-transfer invariance prevents a change of representation from being counted as a capability expansion. An executable Boolean-program repair agent makes the distinction concrete: over 36,864 paired runs, counterexample feedback reduces verifier calls without changing coverage, whereas an enforced permission change admits a new target with a proof excluding every old-interface program. Exact and uniformly gapped randomized verification share this account; independent majority amplification improves reliability while preserving the accepted language. Separate adaptive-selection contracts state what is additionally required to interpret a proposed successor's score as evidence of deployment improvement. Classical hierarchy results and finite audits provide supporting boundaries. The framework specifies the evidence needed to establish improved search, wider accepted capability, and reliable successor selection.

open_alex.title: Collusive Stagnation: Do Verifier Agents Break Deadlock, or Join It?
open_alex.abstract: The field's remedy for an unreliable agent is to add another agent: a critic, judge, or verifier, often implicitly assuming that the verifier is an independent observer. It is not: it is another sample from a similar distribution, often the same model family, reading a context the first agent wrote. We ask whether adding a verifier to a stalling agent restores progress, or whether the pair stalls together in a richer and more expensive way. We identify and name two joint failure modes. In collusive approval the verifier accepts a solution still far from a correct fix, so the system halts and reports success on work that has not reached one. In revision ping-pong the verifier rejects, the coder rephrases rather than rethinks, and the pair can loop to its cap with every step looking like work. We formalize liveness over the dyad's joint state and ground progress in a reference-anchored signal, so that "the verifier approved a submission still distant from a fix" is a mechanically checkable event, and we run a 3x2x2 factorial over verifier relatedness, interaction protocol and cycle cap across 1800 dyad runs. The signal itself has to be audited first, and that is our first result: a blinded adjudicator, the only one of five candidates to reach 0.800 on both halves of a control of patches whose answer was known, puts the corrected rate at about one approval in seven where the raw proxy says seven in ten, while the repositories' own tests, run on 24 flagged approvals, imply 0.517 [0.369, 0.649], so the audit instrument over-credits in its turn. Two counts need no proxy at all: 56.9% of approvals are issued with no revision ever requested, and in 78 runs both agents repeated themselves verbatim until the budget was gone. Swapping the verifier changes which way the dyad fails; we detect no accompanying change in how much an approval is worth, though differences up to 0.20 remain compatible with our data. Against a threshold-perfect critic a real verifier captures 0.342 of the available headroom while ping-pong rises, so inaccurate approval is not necessary for it. Contrary to our own hypothesis, single-agent stop-signals are not structurally blind to dyad-level stagnation.

open_alex.title: PatchPilot: Diff-Gated Dependency Vulnerability Remediation with Deterministic Planning and Bounded Model-Assisted Source Repair
open_alex.abstract: Abstract Third-party dependency vulnerabilities are de- tected reliably but repaired badly. Scanners identify the ad- visory and point at a fixed version range; they rarely establish whether the upgrade is safe for the project that consumes it, and almost never repair the source code that the upgrade breaks. Recent work responds by delegating the decision to large language model (LLM) agents, yet a large-scale study of agent-authored pull requests finds that agents select already- vulnerable versions more often than humans do, and that remediating those selections disproportionately requires major- version upgrades. A benchmark of 203 real dependency-upgrade tasks reports that the strongest coding-agent configuration completes barely half of them, with the dominant failure being an incomplete repository-wide migration. This paper presents PatchPilot, a Visual Studio Code exten- sion for the npm, Apache Maven and Python/PyPI ecosystems that deliberately separates three decision authorities which existing tools conflate: version selection, source repair and build adjudication. Version selection is fully deterministic— computed from registry metadata and Open Source Vulnera- bilities (OSV) advisory evidence, restricted to exact version pins, and rendered as a reviewable diff before any byte is written. Build adjudication belongs to the project’s own test commands, executed without a shell from a fixed template table. Source repair is the only task delegated to a model, and it is confined by a hard never-editable manifest boundary, a path allowlist, exact-once edit semantics and byte budgets, behind a per-request consent gate. Every write is preceded by a SHA-256 snapshot, so rollback restores byte-identical content and detects files the developer edited in the meantime. We evaluate PatchPilot as a design-science artifact: we state the invariants the architecture is required to satisfy, trace each to its implementing mechanism, and verify them through 252 pure unit tests that run without VS Code or network access, extension-host smoke tests, four reproducible sample projects and a headless end-to-end runner. We report the properties that hold by construction, identify the security properties that do not hold, and outline the benchmark-based empirical evaluation that remains future work.

open_alex.title: Yuga: Automatically Detecting Lifetime Annotation Bugs in the Rust Language
open_alex.abstract: The Rust programming language is becoming increasingly popular among systems programmers due to its efficient performance and robust memory safety guarantees. Rust employs an ownership model to ensure these guarantees by allowing each value to be owned by only one identifier at a time. It uses the concept of borrowing and lifetimes to enable other variables to temporarily borrow values. Despite its benefits, security vulnerabilities have been reported in Rust projects, often attributed to the use of “unsafe” Rust code. These vulnerabilities, in part, arise from incorrect lifetime annotations on function signatures. However, existing tools fail to detect these bugs, primarily because such bugs are rare, challenging to detect through dynamic analysis, and require explicit memory models. To overcome these limitations, we characterize incorrect lifetime annotations as a source of memory safety bugs and leverage this understanding to devise a novel static analysis tool,Yuga, to detect potential lifetime annotation bugs.Yugauses a multi-phase analysis approach, starting with a quick pattern-matching algorithm to identify potential buggy components and then conducting a flow and field-sensitive alias analysis to confirm the bugs. We also curate new datasets of lifetime annotation bugs.Yugasuccessfully detects bugs with good precision on these datasets, and we make the code and datasets publicly available.

open_alex.title: TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
open_alex.abstract: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging.Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure.However, progress faces two main challenges.First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context.Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors whose downstream effects differ: some are repaired, some remain harmless, and only some contribute to the final failure.In this work, we propose TRA-JDEBUG, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error's resolution status and terminal impact.We further construct TRAJERRBENCH, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from τ 2 -Benchand SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios.Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TRAJDEBUG achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success.We will release the code and data to facilitate further research 1 .

open_alex.title: Your Agents Are Aging Too: Agent Lifespan Engineering for Deployed Systems
open_alex.abstract: Long-lived AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent operational systems, yet they are still mostly evaluated like freshly initialized models. Day-one benchmarks miss a basic systems question: how does an agent's reliability change after deployment? Even when model weights are frozen, an agent's effective state keeps changing as it compresses interaction history, retrieves from a growing memory store, revises facts after updates, and undergoes routine maintenance. Reliability therefore becomes a lifespan property of the full agent harness, not only a snapshot property of the base model. We introduce AgingBench, a longitudinal reliability benchmark for agent lifespan engineering: measuring not only whether deployed agents degrade, but what form the degradation takes and where repair should target. AgingBench organizes agent aging into four mechanisms: compression aging, where writing and rewriting drops future-relevant details; interference aging, where accumulated similar memories crowd out the target fact; revision aging, where changed or derived state is not updated correctly; and maintenance aging, where lifecycle events such as model swapping trigger regressions. To diagnose these failures, AgingBench uses temporal dependency graphs and counterfactual probes that produce diagnostic profiles for the write, retrieval, and utilization stages of the memory pipeline. Across 6 scenarios, 10 memory systems and 6 models from two families, we find that agent aging is not one-dimensional over 400 runs spanning 50-200 sessions: a well-formed reply can hide a value the memory no longer supplies; derived state collapses as updates accumulate; and the same wrong answer can require different repairs depending on what the diagnostic profile points to.

open_alex.title: Miri: Practical Undefined Behavior Detection for Rust
open_alex.abstract: The Rust programming language has two faces: on the one hand, it is a high-level language with a strong type system ensuring memory and thread safety. On the other hand, Rust crucially relies on unsafe code for cases where the compiler is unable to statically ensure basic safety properties. The challenges of writing unsafe Rust are similar to those of writing C or C++: a single mistake in the program can lead to Undefined Behavior , which means the program is no longer described by the language's Abstract Machine and can go wrong in arbitrary ways, often causing security issues. Ensuring the absence of Undefined Behavior bugs is therefore a high priority for unsafe Rust authors. In this paper we present Miri , the first tool that can find all de-facto Undefined Behavior in deterministic Rust programs. Some of the key non-trivial features of Miri include tracking of pointer provenance, validation of Rust type invariants, data-race detection, exploration of weak memory behaviors, and implementing enough basic OS APIs (such as file system access and concurrency primitives) to be able to run unchanged real-world Rust code. In an evaluation on more than 100 000 Rust libraries, Miri was able to successfully execute more than 70% of the tests across their combined test suites. Miri has found dozens of real-world bugs and has been integrated into the continuous integration of the Rust standard library and many prominent Rust libraries, preventing many more bugs from ever entering these codebases.
open_alex.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages

open_alex.title: ERASan: Efficient Rust Address Sanitizer
open_alex.abstract: Rust is a rapidly growing system programming language that ensures a speed comparable to traditional C/C++ system programming languages, along with the additional benefit of guaranteed memory safety. However, Rust’s strict security rules make implementing and executing some features challenging. To address this, Rust has introduced unsafe Rust, which is less constrained by these strict rules. Nevertheless, these unsafe Rust, where strict Rust security rules are not fully applied, can cause temporal and spatial memory bugs that account for 22% of the Rust bugs reported between 2016 and 2023.In this paper, we propose an efficient address sanitizer design customized for Rust, called ERASan, to detect memory bugs in Rust programs more efficiently than prior work. Based on our thorough analysis of safe and unsafe Rust programming language standards as well as memory bugs found in real-world Rust programs over the past years, we design and implement ERASan to only instrument memory accesses in both safe and unsafe code areas where Rust cannot guarantee safety. We evaluate ERASan with several real-world applications. ERASan removes an average of 90.03% of ASan’s memory access checks. Due to this, ERASan significantly reduces ASan’s performance overhead by an average of 239.05% without harming its bug-finding ability.

open_alex.title: RustMizan: A Compilable, Contamination-Aware Benchmarking Framework for Rust Vulnerabilities
open_alex.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly applied to vulnerability analysis, but existing benchmarks have not kept pace. They typically rely on small non-compilable snippets, focus on binary classification (vulnerable or not), and do not account for the risk that publicly-released datasets are part of model training corpora. We introduce RustMizan, a benchmarking framework for Rust vulnerability analysis that addresses these gaps. RustMizan contains compilable code variants at the crate, file, and function levels, with annotations for binary vulnerability detection, CWE classification, and function- and line-level localization. A paired mutation framework produces semantics-preserving code mutants for contamination testing and robustness probing. Across four frontier models in an agentic setup with command-line access, binary classification sits in the 56-65% range, but line localization F1 stays near 20%, and adversarial cues drop line F1 by about 27%.
open_alex.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

open_alex.title: A Study of Undefined Behavior Across Foreign Function Boundaries in Rust Libraries
open_alex.abstract: Developers rely on the static safety guarantees of the Rust programming language to write secure and performant applications. However, Rust is frequently used to interoperate with other languages which allow design patterns that conflict with Rust's evolving aliasing models. Miri is currently the only dynamic analysis tool that can validate applications against these models, but it does not support finding bugs in foreign functions, indicating that there may be a critical correctness gap across the Rust ecosystem. We conducted a large-scale evaluation of Rust libraries that call foreign functions to determine whether Miri's dynamic analyses remain useful in this context. We used Miri and an LLVM interpreter to jointly execute applications that call foreign functions, where we found 46 instances of undefined or undesired behavior in 37 libraries. Three bugs were found in libraries that had more than 10,000 daily downloads on average during our observation period, and one was found in a library maintained by the Rust Project. Many of these bugs were violations of Rust's aliasing models, but the latest Tree Borrows model was significantly more permissive than the earlier Stacked Borrows model. The Rust community must invest in new, production-ready tooling for multi-language applications to ensure that developers can detect these errors.

open_alex.title: Mem-RAG Artifact
open_alex.abstract: # Mem-RAG Mem-RAG is a Rust static analyzer for unsafe-code bugs whose safety depends on type properties. It runs as a custom `rustc` driver through a Cargo wrapper and analyzes MIR to report contract violations in generic and non-generic Rust code. Mem-RAG focuses on three bug classes: - **Layout**: invalid assumptions about size, alignment, padding, representation, or zero-sized types. - **Validity**: constructing or exposing values whose bytes may violate Rust validity or initialization requirements. - **Ownership**: duplicating non-`Copy` ownership through raw copies, leading to double-drop or use-after-move risks. ## Install Mem-RAG uses `rustc_private`, so use the pinned nightly toolchain: ```bash rustup toolchain install nightly-2025-08-05 rustup component add --toolchain nightly-2025-08-05 rustc-dev llvm-tools-preview ``` Python 3 is required for the batch CSV scanners. ## Analyze One Crate From inside a Rust crate: ```bash /path/to/Mem-RAG/scripts/run_cargo_rvigil.sh -- -- -Zanalysis-mode interprocedural ``` Or by manifest path: ```bash /path/to/Mem-RAG/scripts/run_cargo_rvigil.sh \ --manifest-path /path/to/crate/Cargo.toml \ -- -- -Zanalysis-mode interprocedural ``` Useful analyzer options: ```text -Zanalysis-mode interprocedural -Zanalysis-mode intraprocedural -Zallow-may -Zsensitivity-high -Zsensitivity-med -Zsensitivity-low -Zprint-sinks -Zenable-optional-range-sinks ``` ## Scan CSV Inputs Scan `crate.csv`: ```bash ./scripts/scan_crate_csv.sh ``` Scan `benchmark.csv`: ```bash ./scripts/scan_benchmark_csv.sh ``` Both scanners accept normal runner options, for example: ```bash ./scripts/scan_crate_csv.sh --max-crates 100 --out-dir results/crate_scan ./scripts/scan_benchmark_csv.sh --max-samples 10 --out-dir results/benchmark_scan ``` Outputs are written under `results/` by default, including `results.csv`, `summary.json`, logs, crate caches, and temporary analysis work directories. ## Examples `tests/cases/` contains small Rust crates for Mem-RAG's target bug classes: ```text layout_zst_vec_from_raw_parts layout_padding_exposure layout_misaligned_packed_read validity_zeroed_nonzero ownership_ptr_read_double_drop ``` Run one example: ```bash cd tests/cases/validity_zeroed_nonzero ../../../scripts/run_cargo_rvigil.sh -- -- -Zanalysis-mode interprocedural -Zallow-may ``` ## Scripts ```text scripts/run_cargo_rvigil.sh scripts/scan_crate_csv.sh scripts/scan_benchmark_csv.sh scripts/run_top_crates_scan.py scripts/run_type_property_benchmark.py ``` ## Development Run Rust unit tests: ```bash cargo +nightly-2025-08-05 test --lib ``` ## open_alex.title: AgentChaosBench: Benchmarking External Fault Detection and Localization in Agentic Systems
open_alex.abstract: Reliability in LLM-based agentic systems is a property of the whole execution (its tool calls, model calls, guardrails, and inter-agent messages), not of the final answer alone, yet evaluating only task outcomes reveals little about how or why a run fails. We present AgentChaosBench, a benchmark for detecting and localizing runtime faults in agentic systems from their execution telemetry. We run five heterogeneous applications that coordinate agents over the Agent-to-Agent protocol and call tools through the Model Context Protocol, and inject ten types of operational fault (unavailable or slow tools, corrupted or oversized responses, and delayed, looped, or misrouted delegations and bypassed guardrails) at their tool, model, guardrail, and inter-agent boundaries, alongside a no-fault control. The resulting dataset contains 275 sanitized traces: 250 faulty executions spanning ten fault types and 25 no-fault controls. Each faulty trace is aligned with the no-fault execution of the same input; fault-type labels and, where applicable, location labels are held out from diagnosis. On structured single-trace inputs, a first set of zero-shot LLM baselines shows the task is far from solved: local detectors up to 14B parameters reach only 13.6–19.2% top-1 fault-type accuracy and the frontier DeepSeek-v4-pro only 24.8%, while jointly identifying the fault type and its location tops out at 22%; reference-dependent faults (above all a bypassed guardrail) stay near-unsolved from a single trace. An aligned reference improves selected relative faults but does not resolve guardrail bypass. The held-out labels and compact prediction format support reproducible comparison of LLM-based and non-LLM diagnosis methods.

open_alex.title: Verified Implementation of the Next-gen Borrow Checking Algorithm for Rust via Abstract Interpretation
open_alex.abstract: Borrow checking is a central mechanism for Rust to ensure temporal memory safety. Its correctness is based on the intuition that the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline guarantees that programs without borrow errors inherently could not access invalid references (i.e., pointers). However, existing work on formalizing borrow checking treats it either as a component of type systems or as symbolic execution describing resource transfer. None provides a direct explanation of the correctness of borrow checking algorithms such as Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL) or Polonius in the official Rust compiler that function more like static pointer analysis. We take a first step toward solving this problem by formalizing Polonius, the next-generation borrow- checking algorithm for the Rust compiler, on a core subset of Rust. We prove its correctness by showing that any program accepted by Polonius does not access invalid references at runtime. The key observation is that, when borrow checking is performed lazily, Polonius could be treated as a forward abstract interpretation on abstract domains recording pointer aliasing (borrowing) relations. By providing a concrete semantics that formally describes the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline, we prove the soundness of this abstract interpretation, from which we derive memory safety of checked programs. This formulation of Polonius is implemented and formally verified in the abstract interpretation framework of CompCert. The correctness proofs are generated by an agentic AI under human guidance using paper proofs as proof outline. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive formalization and verification of a borrow checking algorithm as manifested in the Rust compiler.

open_alex.title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification
open_alex.abstract: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.

open_alex.title: PatchTrust: software patch acceptance data with task and process evidence
open_alex.abstract: PatchTrust contains 210 complete task–patch pairs from 150 repositories across Python, JavaScript, TypeScript and Go. Each record links a three-category acceptance decision (accept, human review or block) to six scoped assessment dimensions: task constraints, functional behaviour, test integrity, security, dependencies and generation trajectory. PatchTrust-data.zip provides selected task and candidate-patch files, record identities, adopted labels, substantive review reasons, current paired/adjudicated results where applicable, selected trajectory and source-context evidence, field definitions and source attribution. The main decisions are 133 accept, 41 human review and 36 block. There are 1,260 dimension states, 8,046 event excerpts and 50,142 exported source/context lines. PatchTrust-code.zip provides standard-library Python readers, verification modules and a descriptive-statistics reproduction script, with usage instructions and integrity manifests. It loads and checks the prepared collection without executing commands from research records. Python 3.11 or newer is required; no model API key or paid service is needed. Join records by review_id and cross-check sample_id. Annotation notes retain Chinese text; source material retains its original language, with English field and assessment definitions supplied. Evidence is distributed as selected excerpts; source locations, omitted references and review-rule cohorts are explicitly recorded. Consult the annotation guide for each judgment's scope. open_alex.title: Collusive Stagnation: Do Verifier Agents Break Deadlock, or Join It?
open_alex.abstract: The field's remedy for an unreliable agent is to add another agent: a critic, judge, or verifier, often implicitly assuming that the verifier is an independent observer. It is not: it is another sample from a similar distribution, often the same model family, reading a context the first agent wrote. We ask whether adding a verifier to a stalling agent restores progress, or whether the pair stalls together in a richer and more expensive way. We identify and name two joint failure modes. In collusive approval the verifier accepts a solution still far from a correct fix, so the system halts and reports success on work that has not reached one. In revision ping-pong the verifier rejects, the coder rephrases rather than rethinks, and the pair can loop to its cap with every step looking like work. We formalize liveness over the dyad's joint state and ground progress in a reference-anchored signal, so that "the verifier approved a submission still distant from a fix" is a mechanically checkable event, and we run a 3x2x2 factorial over verifier relatedness, interaction protocol and cycle cap across 1800 dyad runs. The signal itself has to be audited first, and that is our first result: a blinded adjudicator, the only one of five candidates to reach 0.800 on both halves of a control of patches whose answer was known, puts the corrected rate at about one approval in seven where the raw proxy says seven in ten, while the repositories' own tests, run on 24 flagged approvals, imply 0.517 [0.369, 0.649], so the audit instrument over-credits in its turn. Two counts need no proxy at all: 56.9% of approvals are issued with no revision ever requested, and in 78 runs both agents repeated themselves verbatim until the budget was gone. Swapping the verifier changes which way the dyad fails; we detect no accompanying change in how much an approval is worth, though differences up to 0.20 remain compatible with our data. Against a threshold-perfect critic a real verifier captures 0.342 of the available headroom while ping-pong rises, so inaccurate approval is not necessary for it. Contrary to our own hypothesis, single-agent stop-signals are not structurally blind to dyad-level stagnation.

open_alex.title: agent-evidence-vectors: conformance vectors for agent execution evidence
open_alex.abstract: Conformance vectors for agent execution evidence, and the reference verifier that judges them. This release carries 49 corpus manifests across 48 suites and 2,476 vectors in all, among them the in-toto adversarial-execution-evidence predicate, the in-toto ai-agent-action predicate, an AI generation predicate, the observed-effect predicate, SCITT COSE carriage, signed decision receipts and receipt chains, an anchor-stream verifier, ACS core, artifact binding, MCP response-phase interception, the OWASP MCP verification draft, the W3C per-check reporting format and intake, A2A agent-card canonicalization, delegation lifecycle, authority at dispatch, done contracts and receipts, grader isolation, spoofed tool output, test tampering, ACI deployments, and uncertain-effect cases. One binary judges every one of them, selected by the suite each corpus manifest declares. Each corpus digest is listed, recomputed from the vector files, in CORPUS-DIGESTS.txt, which the GitHub release signs and timestamps. The predicate's model is execute-and-attest rather than match-and-assert: a consumer recomputes the outcome from the bytes the statement carries, instead of trusting a verdict the producer asserted about itself. This repository is a second, independently usable implementation of that contract, so that any producer of the predicate type can self-certify and any consumer can reject a lying emitter. For the adversarial-execution-evidence corpus this deposit covers suite revision 32: 288 vectors, of which 63 accept, 223 reject and 2 are indeterminate. Its bytes are fixed by the corpus digest bf3e5befd71640757ff1b3f0af63507364b823b5e3f9059678f72f64a46e11c1 recorded in vectors/MANIFEST.json. A published revision is never mutated in place; a normative change to the predicate, or an addition to the corpus, bumps the revision and regenerates every vector byte-identically from its generators, because the vendored specification's digest is itself a corpus input. The archive is the output of git archive --format=tar.gz --prefix=agent-evidence-vectors-0.30.0/ v0.30.0 and reproduces byte for byte from the signed tag (SHA-256 30f8e11c511a7fd61f4b63944e6ab71e2eb97f4544a05df3cbe73ea0f283303c). The intended use is citation by a conformance requirement. A requirement that names this suite, or any other suite demonstrated to exercise the same conditions, is checkable by a party who trusts neither the producer nor the implementer. Cite this version DOI for a conformance claim; the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22758687 always resolves to the newest release.

open_alex.title: Who Defines Sense: Specification Authority and the Presence-Absence Asymmetry in Agentic Verification
open_alex.abstract: Agentic verification systems increasingly rely on reviewer models, tool calls, gates, and repeated audit loops. These systems can check many properties of a declared task representation, but the representation itself must first make the relevant properties available for audit. This paper argues that agentic verification requires a distinct role of specification authority: the function that determines what the verifier must be able to inspect before verification begins.The argument extends the specification-boundary framework introduced in "Why Sense Matters" and the specification-boundary engineering results of "How Sense Works." Through controlled reviewer tests derived from citation-verification failures, the paper shows that audit reliability depends on more than adding another reviewer. In a fix-verify architecture test, centralized self-review returned PASS while separated verification with a claim-evidence map returned HOLD on an unresolved historical-reference disclosure problem. In a 12-output 2 x 2 replication, PASS/HOLD verdicts varied across repetitions, but claim-evidence maps more reliably localized the historical-reference-file manifest and answer-key/seeding fields as the relevant evidence object.The paper then reports a 3 x 3 diagnostic reviewer matrix crossing three reviewer rows with three blinded boundary-defect stimuli. All nine cells produced HOLD; the same verdict label carried different diagnostic content across reviewers. Visible direct answer-key exposure and visible proxy-field leakage were precisely identified by some reviewer rows, while the omitted historical field manifest received only broad missing-evidence treatment. A targeted rule-strength expansion then isolates a consequence-layer effect: in a fresh paired OpenAI API rerun using the dated snapshot gpt-5.5-2026-04-23, a weak asymmetric rule produced PASS with the clean-reference manifest marked PARTIAL, while a strong symmetric rule assigning release-blocking force to the same gap produced HOLD with blocker CLEAN_MANIFEST. A schema-controlled homogeneous replication strengthened and narrowed this result: GPT-5.5 reproduced the clean flip across three paired reruns, while Grok 4.3 and DeepSeek routes showed model-contingent over-enforcement and field-level inconsistencies.The contribution is a role-level account of agentic verification: reliable audit requires separated definition, execution, verification, and release functions, bound by explicit evidence maps, output schemas, and consequence rules that name which prohibited fields, proxy fields, missing manifests, and evidence objects block interpretation.

open_alex.title: SEVRA-BENCH: Social Engineering of Vulnerabilities in Review Agents
open_alex.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in automated code-review systems, where their approvals can determine which code is merged into shared repositories. However, it is unclear whether review agents can detect vulnerability-introducing code when an attacker controls both the code change and the persuasive Pull Request (PR) narrative designed to mask it. We introduce SEVRA-BENCH (Social Engineering of Vulnerabilities in Review Agents), a benchmark that measures how often a review agent approves such adversarial PR s. Each PR in SEVRA-BENCH is built from a historical commit that fixed a vulnerability. We automatically reverse that fix to extract the original vulnerable code, and submit the resulting code change as a PR wrapped in one of 15 social-engineering framings. To test review-agent resilience to narrative manipulation, these framings vary dimensions such as supporting evidence, conveyed urgency, signals of prior approval, and appeals to authority. SEVRA-BENCH evaluates a retained challenge split of roughly 1000 adversarial PRs drawn from publicly disclosed vulnerability fixes across the top 10 entries of the MITRE's 2025 most dangerous software weaknesses. Evaluating 8 review agents against this benchmark, we reveal that review agents are susceptible to narrative manipulation, exposing a significant gap in security capabilities.

open_alex.title: VATE: Verifier-Side Admission and Evidence Linkage for AI Agent Actions
open_alex.abstract: AI agents can present valid authority yet submit a request that the receiving service must narrow or refuse under its own policy. Reviewing actions across services also requires distinguishing the request admitted from evidence of the subsequent effects. This report presents the Verifiable Agent Trust Envelope (VATE), a verifier-side admission and receipt profile for consequential agent actions, including payments, data updates and permission changes. VATE specifies allow, attenuate and deny decisions, original and effective request relationships, and separate admission and post-execution records. At v0.4.0, its fixed comparison corpus contains 76 cases. Four external project accounts examine freshness enforcement, request binding, consistency of signed payment artifacts, and interpretation of receipt constraints. Two native refusal experiments, each covering one partial case, were replayed against v0.4.0; historical comparison and adapter-feedback records address the other questions. The accounts identify concrete agreements, reporting differences and input-contract changes needed to relate native behavior to shared assertions. They also show how an implementation's feedback can clarify the reporting contract itself. The demonstrated native behavior covers refusal paths, while checks of declared narrowing and post-execution linkage use reference fixtures and submitted artifact comparisons. VATE provides a design and evaluation reference for implementers deciding what must be bound, enforced and recorded at an action boundary and what another party needs to inspect afterward. The evaluated software snapshot is VATE v0.4.0. The v0.4.1 archive also contains the cited Vaara and Bolyra run records with their original evaluation pins. Supplement S1 contains two saved repository self-test reports, checksums and reproduction commands. The report text and original tables are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The source build script and Supplement S1 retain Apache-2.0.

open_alex.title: Who Verifies the Agents? A Case Series of Unsupported Verification Verdicts
open_alex.abstract: Corrected camera-ready version. The text first accepted at the workshop had two wrong case accounts; this version corrects them and answers the reviewers. We nearly submitted a false example. One agent reported that a released CI tool passed an empty repository. A second installed the package and found that the defect had already been fixed. Our draft described a release we had not tested. We report a case series of six software systems in a coding-agent workflow, with different levels of evidence. The cases include checks over empty inputs, an error page treated as a deployment, a source-inspected review queue, and boundary cases. After acceptance we recovered the original session records. They corrected two of our own accounts and filled one gap. The deployment monitor hashed an error page on two recorded checks, not for a day. The job scanner's earlier state already used the correct source, so no false new-role verdict is established. The identity command's declarations were briefly counted as verified, then falsified inside the workflow. These are related evidence problems, not six established instances of an identical failure. Five systems share an operator and toolchain; the external job-board endpoint is third-party, but its interpretation also belongs to that operator's workflow. The series supports a description of mechanisms, not an incidence estimate or a causal comparison of agent architectures. A further detector encountered three failures while looking for this family of errors, including a failed history read reported as a count of zero. We recommend that verification name its target and coverage, distinguish measurement failure from a negative result, and demonstrate that its control can fail for the intended reason. Independent review helped in these cases, but we do not establish that a second agent is necessary or sufficient. Historical commands and outputs are included, with a per-case provenance table that separates recorded, reconstructed and missing fields. Dated local replays reproduce the CI defect and fix, exercise three historical detector tests, and check the original hold-back guard on a historical input projection; they are new executions, not original evidence. Only the external endpoint has public query addresses supplied here. We also describe an unrun comparison design and the limits of its proposed sample size.

open_alex.title: The Model Proposes, the Code Disposes: A Pre-Registered Ablation of a Verifier-and-Acceptance Stage in an LLM-Orchestrated Offensive-Security Agent
open_alex.abstract: We evaluate whether a verifier-and-acceptance stage - a model verifier whose verdicts are enforced by deterministic code - changes what an LLM-driven offensive-security agent reports. We report a 15-run exploratory pilot, a pre-registered 20-run confirmatory ablation, and a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial study with 40 runs across two deliberately vulnerable lab targets. In the confirmatory study, removing the stage eliminated pre-report suppression (median 2 versus 0 findings per run; exact one-sided p = 0.00003) and reduced model-blinded shipped precision (median 0.471 versus 0.353; p = 0.0087). Recall against a frozen but incomplete ground-truth list did not differ significantly (two-sided p = 0.158; equivalence was not established). The factorial study attributed suppression to the model verifier (Holm-adjusted p = 0.004); deterministic acceptance rules alone suppressed no false positives, and no interaction was detected (p = 0.72). The full design retained 93.8% of model-adjudicated true candidates but did not meet its pre-registered non-inferiority criterion because the lower one-sided 95% bound was 0.875, below the 0.90 floor. Across the confirmatory and factorial studies, an instrumented canary recorded zero contacts in 60 of 60 runs, with incidental external contacts disclosed separately. Independent human adjudication of the retained blind packets is pending, so precision and sensitivity endpoints are supporting rather than final evidence. Six audit-trail failures, including one in the evaluation tooling, are also disclosed. The results support a narrow conclusion: the verifier changes what the system ships, while deterministic code supplies enforcement and auditability; they do not establish superiority to other agents or generalization beyond lab targets.

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise cognitive networking lacks a shared, leakage-safe benchmark that couples multi-layer configuration, multi-modal telemetry, and supervised NetOps labels. We present ECNetBench, a synthetic enterprise benchmark under AOS-CX-style operational assumptions, and an Enterprise Cognitive Network (ECN-v3) with Perception, Anomaly, Prediction, RCA, Impact, and Healing agents. The final T1 detector combines leakage-safe temporal enrichment with anchored telemetry-first fusion; nesting-safe stacking is retained only as a negative ablation. On six frozen instances with a temporal 70/15/15 protocol, ECN-v3 attains mean T1 AUPRC 0.115 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.068, 0.168]), above random forest (0.076) and the prior v2 configuration (0.058), while paired tests versus RF remain non-significant at n=6. The recommended T2 head is telemetry logistic regression. The contribution is a reproducible multi-seed benchmark and an evidence-selected detection-RCAhealing decision-support pipeline with honest multi-seed statistics.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Kronumos 2 Kairos: Cost-Bounded Automated Program Repair via Dual-Brain Cybernetic Sub-Cortex on SWE-bench Verified
crossref.abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) in authentic software repositories presents a formidable challenge: models must localize defects within repository contexts, synthesize character-exact syntactic modifications, and preserve regression invariance without corrupting preexisting functionality. In this paper, we present Kronumos 2 Kairos , a cost-bounded autonomous program repair engine coupling a fine-tuned 7B open-weight code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) with the Tokenectomy Dual-Brain Cybernetic Sub-Cortex—a zero-allocation deterministic runtime featuring an Issue De-Noiser, a 9-domain Procedural Cognitive Kernel, an Interlocking Causal Invariant Mesh (ICIM), a Dual-Key Consensus Gate, a Cryptographic SHA-256 Merkle Causal Chain, an Immune Cluster Pattern Classifier, and an AST Auto-Bracket & Indentation Healer. Evaluated against the complete 500-instance Princeton SWE-bench Verified dataset using the official Docker testbed with 100% container execution coverage, Kronumos 2 Kairos synthesized 442 candidate patches while withholding 58 (11.6%) via deterministic structural validation (Zero Dirty Diff). The system verified 8 production bug resolutions across four distinct open-source ecosystems (Django, Scikit-Learn, PyData Xarray, and Sphinx) at strictly $0.00 marginal inference cost and an average of 2,512 tokens per task (a 93.5% token reduction vs. industry multi-turn baselines). Furthermore, an empirical ablation demonstrates that the Sub-Cortex AST Healer alone rescued 2 additional resolutions (+33% improvement over the pre-healing baseline), confirming the architectural necessity of deterministic post-processing in open-weight APR pipelines.

crossref.title: Graph-Evidence Repository Repair: Risk-Calibrated Retrieval and Patch Gating on SWE-Bench
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Repository-scale issue repair requires more than patch generation: it requires evidence retrieval, test-grounded rejection, uncertainty calibration, and an explicit decision about whether a candidate deserves scarce verification capacity. This paper proposes RAGE-Repair, a graph-evidence repair method evaluated with the public SWE-bench Lite corpus. The case study loads 300 SWE-bench Lite instances from 12 repositories and analyzes issue length, patch size, test-patch effort, and changed-file scope. The method constructs a repository evidence lattice, estimates residual ambiguity, penalizes tail patch risk with CVaR, and admits a candidate only when expected repair value exceeds its test and review price. The median problem statement contains 1044 characters, the median gold patch has 20 lines, and the top repository contributes 114 instances. Native derivations establish the robust risk bound, primal-dual capacity controller, online regret guarantee, and graph-specific patch gate. The resulting design makes each accepted or rejected repair traceable to evidence support, uncertainty, and verification cost.</jats:p>

Evaluation of Selected Dynamic Parameters of Rotating Turbocharger Units Based on Comparative Model and Bench Tests
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Obtaining the best operating parameters of the internal combustion engine has focused the attention of designers and researchers since the first years of its creation. Initial research focused on increasing engine power and overall efficiency. As time passed, these aspirations became more sophisticated and began to concern other operating parameters of the drive unit. The basic problem, however, remained the improvement of filling the cylinder with the working medium. Turbocharger charging consists in using the energy of the exhaust gases to drive a turbine placed on a common shaft with a compressor supplying air under increased pressure to the cylinders. Over time, the turbocharger became one of the key elements and its technical condition began to play a key role in the operation and performance of modern drive units. Like every element, the turbocharger itself is not without its faults. This procedure is known among manufacturers who, when designing power units and their assemblies, pay special attention to the essence of turbocharger construction. Since it is impossible to predict all the phenomena accompanying a working turbocharger at the design stage, the authors of this paper conducted bench tests of a selected batch of turbochargers, focusing mainly on the vibration measurements of the turbocharger rotating assembly. At the same time, we present a dynamic model of the mentioned system based on the analyses resulting from the solutions of the equations of a numerical model. In order to give the research a practical aspect, the results of the theoretical research were compared with the results of bench tests. It has been shown that the basic problem is to guarantee the correct operating parameters of the bearings in the position of static and dynamic equilibrium. Obtaining such operating parameters requires finding a compromise solution, e.g., between the maximum temperature in oil films and the amplitudes of vibration accelerations in bearing nodes. The research results presented in the article can be used as a field for further discussion in the field of research on the reliability of turbochargers and be helpful in the design process in order to avoid design errors and reduce production costs.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Service Dependency Intelligence for Contract-aware Agent Design in Enterprise Microservice Architectures
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>LLM-based coding agents designing solutions in enterprise microservice architectures must understand service dependencies, API contracts, and event topologies to produce correct, deployment-safe designs. We present a service dependency intelligence system that constructs and maintains a queryable dependency graph from static code and configuration analysis, enabling agents to perform contract-aware design. The system extracts over 3,200 dependency edges across 74 distinct detection signal types from approximately 900 repositories at a Fortune 50 retailer, queryable in under 500ms via a RediSearch index. Integrated into the agent's design workflow as a mandatory pre-modification step, the system enforces contractaware architecture rules: agents must enumerate all affected consumers, specify backward-compatible migration strategies, and define deployment ordering before proposing any API or event schema change. The dependency graph achieves 100% precision on detected edges (team-validated, zero false positives) with a 5-10% recall gap from scan depth limitations. With over 1,800 total interactions across a conversational AI assistant, catalog browser, and automated design pipelines, the system demonstrates that static dependency intelligence-without runtime instrumentation-provides sufficient context for agents to produce designs that respect the enterprise service topology.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Incremental Repair of Agent Memory and Plans after Business Evidence Revisions
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Business evidence revisions can invalidate an AI agent's facts, drafts and plans at different times. We develop an executable repair contract that separates immutable generation history, current reuse validation and the artifacts due for a particular use. A frozen source-derived study evaluates Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct with six policy configurations and a common four-call flow budget. Its 24 held-out flows comprise 16 main-test and eight airline-transfer flows, yielding 288 policy-model episodes and 864 assigned uses. On the main test, joint reuse preserves graph-local repair's exact root-wise scored outcomes while reducing logical input Tokens by 22.2% for Qwen and 24.1% for Llama. Source re-reading produces more correct uses: 27 versus 26 for Qwen and 29 versus 24 for Llama, each out of 48. Transfer retains the quality-cost trade-off. Independent scoring attributes published errors to plan choice and approval or blocking decisions, including errors retained by otherwise valid reuse. A deterministic reference separates these decision errors from snapshot and record handling; two supporting controlled censuses retain 3,072 and 4,608 assigned uses with complete lifecycle ledgers. The findings establish an operational distinction between current inputs and correct decisions, and show how to evaluate incremental repair against strong re-reading controls using jointly reported correctness, error retention and full-flow cost.</jats:p>

crossref.title: VeriCrypt-Agent: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Verification for Cryptographic Dependency Updates
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Cryptographic dependency updates can install cleanly and pass visible regression tests while changing project-facing behavior or leaving an application inside a vulnerable version range. This study presents VeriCrypt-Agent, an evidence-grounded workflow for bounded-autonomy cryptographic maintenance. The system combines a frozen snapshot of release/advisory evidence, a public catalog of project-level executable probes, cross-version execution under old and candidate dependency versions, role-specialized LLM reasoning, and a deterministic decision gate. Automatic merging is allowed only when mandatory probes pass, policy constraints are satisfied, and the audit record is complete. On CryptoUpdate-Mini-30, ten unique package-version transitions are evaluated through 30 controlled executions. Visible tests accept all five non-mergeable transitions, while advisory-only screening accepts two of five. The deterministic All-Probes Gate performs best on this benchmark, with perfect transition-level decisions and no review cases, when all relevant probes are already known and inexpensive. The full workflow observes no unsafe auto-merges (0/5; exact 95% CI: 0.000–0.522) and routes 9/30 executions to review (0.30; exact 95% CI: 0.147–0.494). Removing grounding accepts three of five non-mergeable transitions, and a fixed probe budget accepts two of five. On 48 blinded static crypto-API audit files, including 32 unsafe cases, two-pass review detects 20/32 unsafe cases (0.625; exact 95% CI: 0.437–0.789) and reaches macro-F1 =0.556. These point estimates characterize evidence-backed release decisions only under the evaluated conditions; they do not establish general superiority over exhaustive deterministic testing or a deployable static vulnerability detector.</jats:p>

crossref.title: SkillGraph: Dependency-Aware Retrieval for Compositional Agent Skills
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>LLM-powered agents increasingly rely on modular skills-reusable packages of instructions, scripts, and resources. With over 280K public skills as of early 2026, the paradigm has proven its value. Yet current systems treat skills as flat, isolated units: indexed by description, retrieved via semantic similarity, and executed independently. We show this flat representation fundamentally limits retrieval accuracy and compositional execution. Our evidence: (1) LLMs exhibit systematic selection bias among large tool sets; (2) real-world workflows follow strong sequential patterns invisible to semantic similarity; and (3) graph-based approaches consistently outperform flat retrieval. We propose SkillGraph-a directed multigraph with five typed edge categories (dependency, co-invocation, prerequisite, conflict, enhancement)-and validate it on 100 software engineering skills with 155 typed edges across 35 queries at four difficulty levels. On compositional queries, SkillGraph achieves 0.60 compositional recall vs. 0.40 for BM25 (+50%); on multi-hop queries, communitybased traversal reaches 0.419 recall vs. 0.187 (+124%).</jats:p>

crossref.title: CAVEAT: Reliability-aware active verification under correlated errors for multi-agent LLM reasoning
crossref.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems improve reasoning reliability by letting several agents solve a task and reconciling their answers through debate or voting, often followed by a verification stage that checks intermediate steps with additional judges or tools. These pipelines assume that agents and verifiers err independently. In practice, agents from the same model family share training data and failure modes, so their verdicts are correlated and repeated same-family checks carry far less evidence than independence suggests. This paper treats verification as a resource-allocation problem under correlated errors and proposes CAVEAT (Correlation-Aware VErification AllocaTion). CAVEAT merges heterogeneous agent traces into a claim dependency graph, models each verifier by Beta-distributed sensitivity and specificity together with a family-level shared-slip rate that yields a closed-form correlated posterior, and greedily selects which claim to verify, by which verifier and when to stop by a cost-normalised value of information. Ignoring correlation inflates posterior log-odds by a design-effect factor 1+(k−1)ρ, and the greedy policy is near-optimal under adaptive submodularity. On six public benchmarks covering claim verification, multi-hop question answering and mathematical reasoning, with eight heterogeneous verifiers, CAVEAT matches exhaustive verification at 21% of its cost, improves accuracy over the strongest budget-matched baseline by 3.1 points, reduces expected calibration error from 7.4% to 3.8% and lowers the rate of confidently accepted wrong answers from 19.6% to 7.2%.

crossref.title: Mitigating Hallucination Cascades in Multi-Agent Systems via Consensus-Aware Knowledge Verification
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex task automation. However, these systems suffer from a critical vulnerability: hallucination cascade, where erroneous information generated by one agent propagates through the system and is amplified by downstream agents. We propose Dynamic Consensus Auditing (DCA), a novel framework that introduces a lightweight audit agent to monitor inter-agent message flows. DCA combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with uncertainty quantification based on semantic entropy to detect potentially hallucinated content. When high-uncertainty messages are detected, DCA triggers a peer review mechanism where multiple agents vote on the validity of the information. Experiments on HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and MuSiQue benchmarks demonstrate that DCA reduces error propagation rates by 42.5% (relative reduction) on average compared to baseline multi-agent systems, with a token overhead of 15.3% (averaged across datasets). Our results suggest that, in the context of multi-hop question answering with three-agent pipelines, consensus-aware verification provides a practical balance between reliability and computational efficiency in multi-agent collaboration.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Towards a Rust-Like Borrow Checker for C
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Memory safety issues in C are the origin of various vulnerabilities that can compromise a program’s correctness or safety from attacks. We propose an approach to tackle memory safety by replicating Rust’s Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) Borrow Checker. Our solution uses static analysis and successive source-to-source code transformations to be composed upstream of the compiler, ensuring maximal compatibility with existing build systems. This allows us to apply the memory safety guarantees of the rustc compiler to C code with fewer changes than a rewrite in Rust. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of Rust’s efforts towards ensuring memory safety, and describe the theoretical basis for a C borrow checker, alongside a proof-of-concept that was developed to demonstrate its potential. We have evaluated the prototype on the CHStone and bzip2 benchmarks. This prototype correctly identified violations of the ownership and aliasing rules, and exposed incompatibilities between such rules and common C patterns, which can be addressed in future work.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Spell checking is the task of detecting and correcting spelling errors in text and is one of the most sought-after processes in NLP. There are many open-source toolkits for checking and correcting errors in the text. To test how effective these tools are, in this article I have presented an evaluation of three types of tools as NeuSpell, SymSpell and Hunspell. SymSpell showed a high speed of 2480, this is an indicator of how fast it works than others. And NeuSpell achieved the lowest error rate of 0.80%. The results show the disadvantages and advantages of all algorithms, and that there is still room for improvement. </jats:p>

Multi-Agent "Solver-Critic-Checker" Architectures for Reliable Reasoning on GSM8K
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>This research addresses arithmetic hallucinations and cascading logical errors in Large Language Models (LLMs) during multi-step mathematical problem solving. While Transformer-based architectures demonstrate strong natural language capabilities, probabilistic token prediction frequently introduces calculation errors that impair reasoning reliability. To overcome these limitations, this thesis presents the Solver-CriticChecker (SCC) framework, an orchestration architecture that decouples linguistic reasoning from deterministic mathematical computation. The system integrates Chainof-Thought (CoT) prompting via a generative Solver agent, an external regularexpressionbased Python Execution Checker for deterministic algebraic validation, and a Critic agent for structural logic evaluation. The framework was evaluated on consumergrade local hardware using two open weight language models: Qwen2-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B. Testing was performed on a 150-question subset of the GSM8K dataset (Indices Q50-Q199) under constrained context windows. Empirical results confirm that integrating deterministic execution of anchors significantly enhances reasoning pipeline reliability, elevating overall task accuracy to 88.0% (132/150). Model scale proved critical to verification integrity: increasing parameter capacity from 1.5B to 7B reduced falsepositive verification errors from 84 to 10. These findings demonstrate that delegating symbolic verification to external execution tools provides a scalable, computationally efficient paradigm for dependable mathematical reasoning on edge devices.</jats:p>

crossref.title: EATF-MultiRoot: A Reproducible Verifier and Corpus for AI-Agent Evidence Packages
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>AI-agent systems increasingly produce tool calls, policy decisions and runtime outputs that must later be verified outside the system that generated them. Mutable application logs and single-root registries are weak foundations for this task: they can be unavailable, rewritten, captured by one issuer or dependent on later network lookups. EATF-MultiRoot is a reproducible software artifact for testing multi-root verification of AI-agent action evidence. It builds a ten-case corpus of Agent Evidence Package (AEP) objects using the Agent Trust Framework (EATF), applies a local verifier-policy overlay and produces reasoned accept, reject or indeterminate verdicts. The artifact packages the corpus generator, verifier policy, evaluation runner, generated evidence packages, JSON/CSV/Markdown results, manifest and a vendored EATF runtime snapshot so that reviewers can rebuild and inspect the experiment offline. The current corpus matches all ten expected verdicts and covers multi-root success, identity substitution, broker downgrade, issuer distrust, stale revocation evidence, cross-policy replay, offline validation, lookup dependency and algorithm migration. The software is intended as a reusable testbed for researchers and practitioners designing verifiable AI-agent evidence workflows.</jats:p>

STEP-VERIFIER: Learning to Verify Intermediate Agent Behavior with Process Reward Models
crossref.abstract: Large language model agents complete tasks through long sequences of tool calls, yet most training signals only indicate whether the entire attempt succeeded. We explore whether a separate verifier can learn to judge the quality of individual actions before an episode finishes. Our system, STEP-VERIFIER, scores each environment-observation and action pair instead of whole trajectories. It is trained on automatically synthesized comparisons distilled from a success-labeled corpus of logged interactions: Monte-Carlo return differences between states sharing a common prefix yield pairwise supervision, and a Bradley-Terry ranking head converts these pairs into calibrated per-action scores. While the policy is being learned, the verifier filters low-quality interaction logs before each update and provides dense intermediate feedback that is annealed toward zero as training progresses, so the final policy never relies on the verifier at deployment. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct backbones, STEP-VERIFIER outperforms training from final scores alone across GAIA, ToolBench, and AgentBoard, and its per-action scores align substantially better with human judgments than trajectory-level scoring baselines.

crossref.title: Adversarial Evidence-Plane Robustness for Bounded Agent Assurance:Deterministic Mutation Testing of Claim Admissibility
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Assurance for autonomous agents depends on operational evidence about policy decisions, actions, execution, effects, provenance, and enforcement. This study tests whether bounded assurance claims remain semantically admissible when that evidence is adversarially degraded. Three co-primary questions address deviation existence (B1), observable action-path reconstruction (B2), and containment/enforcement-boundary localization (B3). A deterministic mutation harness applied 14 frozen single-operator evidence-plane attacks to three known-ground-truth baselines, producing 42 adversarial cases and 126 claim evaluations. A prospectively frozen strongest-safe oracle and closed-world semantic scorer classified the 126 claim evaluations into three predefined categories: exact safe, safe conservative, and unsafe false establishment. All 42 cases were valid. Of the 126 claim evaluations, 56 were exact safe, 47 safe conservative, and 23 unsafe false establishment. The resulting Unsafe False Establishment Rate (UFER) was 23/126 = 0.18254, so the pre-specified zero-UFER target failed. Unsafe outcomes were B1 3/42, B2 19/42, and B3 1/42. Exploratory forensics classified 21 unsafe evaluations as substantive semantic incompatibilities and two as possible scorer-normalization artifacts. The dominant B2 mechanism was global ineligibility after localized evidentiary degradation. These results distinguish semantic safety from information retention: evidence defects must not induce propositions beyond the boundary justified by surviving admissible evidence.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Verifying the Verifier: An Evidence Audit of Five Synthetic Repository Tasks
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Passing a visible test suite does not establish that generated code satisfies a task specification. A second verifier can reduce this gap, but its own tests can also be incomplete. This paper audits the public Repository Agent Reliability Program (RARB), a small collection of five synthetic Python repository tasks. At a pinned source revision, 52 archived attempts comprise 44 recorded passes, five failures and three holds. After normalizing two evidence schemas, 47 attempts have passing public-test observations; three of these receive a failing verifier verdict. Re-execution of the three discordant candidates and one repaired candidate reproduces their recorded public-test and verifier outcomes at the audited revision. An additional, explicitly post hoc counterexample passes every existing event-idempotency gate while incorrectly applying an interleaved duplicate event, increasing a total from the expected 17 to 27. The result demonstrates a coverage gap despite successful qualification against the existing mutation set. The audit also identifies an ambiguous return-value requirement and a schema-dependent metric denominator. These observations support reporting test discordance, qualification scope and evidence provenance separately. The small, uneven and partly adaptive dataset does not support model rankings, population failure rates or general safety claims. AI-use disclosure: OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex was used substantially for source inspection, literature discovery, audit-script and counterexample construction, analysis, drafting and typesetting. The counterexample is audit-generated, not an additional model-trial observation. AI assistance is not an independent human review.</jats:p>

crossref.title: WaveDiff-Patch: Efffcient Adversarial Patch Generation Based on Diffusion Models Integrated with Discrete Wavelet Transform ​
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Addressing a key challenge in current diffusion model-driven adversarial patch generation—the difffculty in balancing aggressiveness, visual naturalness, and high computational costs—this paper proposes a customizable adversarial patch generation method that combines discrete wavelet transform constraints with a lightweight diffusion model. The method employs a lightweight diffusion model, which has undergone block pruning and feature distillation, as the foundation for image reconstruction. By directly optimizing the terminal latent vectors in the diffusion chain, we signiffcantly reduce computational resource consumption and improve generation efffciency. Furthermore, to compensate for the weakened constraint on the naturalness of adversarial patches imposed by text prompts due to the shortening of the latent vector chain during optimisation, we introduce the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which enables a ffne-tuned balance between patch aggressiveness and visual realism at the frequency domain level. Experiments demonstrate that optimizing the terminal latent vectors using a lightweight diffusion model signiffcantly reduces computational redundancy, with the entire optimization process requiring only 1.43 TFLOPs. Compared to Diffpatch, another diffusion-based customizable method, we achieve a 13.5% increase in attack success rate on YOLOv5s. The generated natural adversarial patches achieved an SSIM score of 0.671 and an LPIPS score of 0.144, indicating that our method better balances attackability and naturalness while maintaining image customizability. ​</jats:p>
